title: Growing Mini-Organs in a Dish
endLine: Reprogrammed stem cells self-organize into mini-organs that test tissue, not whole bodies.

scenes.tts: How can you test developing human brain tissue inside a lab? You cannot experiment on a growing human brain. Instead, researchers grow living mini-organs, called organoids, inside a dish.
scenes.caption: How can you test developing human brain tissue inside a lab? You cannot experiment on a growing human brain. Instead, researchers grow living mini-organs, called organoids, inside a dish.
scenes.visual: Schematic: a faint silhouette of a developing human brain hovers above a glowing circular culture dish filling most of the frame; a subtle question mark pulses over the brain, then fades as small drifting cell clusters brighten inside the dish with label 'Organoids'.
scenes.narration: How can you test developing human brain tissue inside a lab? You cannot experiment on a growing human brain. Instead, researchers grow living mini-organs, called organoids, inside a dish.

scenes.visual: Schematic: gentle ripples and slow drifting particles animate across the glowing culture dish while the title 'Growing Mini-Organs in a Dish' holds clearly across the center, then fades.

scenes.tts: Start with a patient's skin cell. A few proteins called transcription factors reset its identity. It becomes an induced pluripotent stem cell, or i P S cell. Pluripotent means it can make every cell type of the body. And it carries that patient's own genome.
scenes.caption: Start with a patient's skin cell. A few proteins called transcription factors reset its identity. It becomes an induced pluripotent stem cell, or iPS cell. Pluripotent means it can make every cell type of the body. And it carries that patient's own genome.
scenes.visual: Schematic (no molecular structures): inside the same culture dish, a flat skin cell glides to center; a few bright signal beads labelled 'Transcription factors' touch it; the flat cell rounds into a luminous sphere labelled 'iPS cell' with branching faded outlines of brain, gut and muscle cells fanning briefly behind it, carrying a bright badge labelled 'Patient genome'.
scenes.narration: Start with a patient's skin cell. A few proteins called transcription factors reset its identity. It becomes an induced pluripotent stem cell, or iPS cell. Pluripotent means it can make every cell type of the body. And it carries that patient's own genome.

scenes.tts: Next, let those stem cells clump and float in the dish. No one places them, yet they sort themselves by self-organization. They form a polarized sheet with a definite inside and outside. Dividing precursors called progenitors line a fluid-filled cavity, while young neurons lie further out.

scenes.visual: Schematic: the iPS cell divides into a floating aggregate inside the same dish; cells drift inward and outward on their own under label 'Self-organization', hollowing a central fluid-filled cavity; dividing cells labelled 'Progenitors' pulse along the inner rim while outer cells sprout short projections as 'Young neurons'.

scenes.tts: Other organoids, like mini-intestines, start from adult tissue stem cells. They are multipotent, making several cell types within one tissue. In 2009, Toshiro Sato and colleagues grew them in Matrigel, a basement-membrane matrix. They added growth factors that keep the stem cells dividing. Here is the rule: stem cells self-organize into mini-organs that model tissue, never whole bodies.

scenes.visual: Schematic (no molecular structures): the same dish shifts to a translucent gel layer labelled 'Matrigel' holding an adult gut stem cell; simple glowing growth-factor dots wash across it, and the cell buds into a looped mini-intestine with several coloured gut cell types; a faint dashed human body silhouette appears beside the dish to contrast partial tissue with a whole body.

scenes.tts: Now pause and test that rule. Suppose a virus stunts a human brain organoid in your dish. Or sugar makes one donor's gut organoid release glutamate. What do those experiments prove, and what can they never show on their own?
scenes.caption: Now pause and test that rule. Suppose a virus stunts a human brain organoid in your dish. Or sugar makes one donor's gut organoid release glutamate. What do those experiments prove, and what can they never show on their own?
scenes.visual: Schematic (no molecular structures): inside the dish, a brain organoid visibly stalls as small dark virus dots land on it, then shifts to a gut organoid releasing glowing glutamate dots when sugar dots arrive; a crisp question banner rises above the dish: 'What can organoids prove—and miss?'

scenes.visual: Schematic: thinking pause; the question 'What can organoids prove—and miss?' stays clearly on screen while the organoid in the dish gently pulses and the faint dashed body silhouette shimmers beside it.

scenes.tts: Organoids show which human cells a virus harms, not pregnancy risk. An old lab virus strain can mislead, so researchers retest epidemic strains in organoids and pregnant mice. In 2022, Buchanan and colleagues saw glutamate release from one donor's gut organoids. That suggests a conserved response, not human behaviour, so checks in native tissue remain vital.

scenes.visual: Schematic: a bright checkmark highlights damaged cells inside the dish while a clean red cross dims the dashed pregnancy and whole-body silhouette; a fading label 'Old lab strain' swaps to 'Epidemic strain' beside a small mouse outline; then the single-donor gut organoid links by an arrow to a strip labelled 'Native tissue' (Buchanan et al., 2022).

scenes.tts: Used with those guards, this method unlocked three discoveries. First, in 2008, Mototsugu Eiraku, Yoshiki Sasai and colleagues floated mouse and human embryonic stem cells. Embryonic stem cells are pluripotent cells from an early embryo. Their clumps built cortical sheets with a definite inside and outside, with no one placing a cell.

scenes.visual: Schematic: the dish resets to floating embryonic stem cell clusters labelled '2008: Eiraku and Sasai'; the clusters smoothly fold into a polarized cortical sheet with a glowing inner cavity, dividing progenitors inside, and young neurons radiating outward.

scenes.tts: Second, organoids pinpointed which human cells Zika virus harms. In March 2016, Guo-li Ming, Hongjun Song and Hengli Tang tracked Zika in human cortical progenitors. It infected progenitors far more readily than stem cells or immature neurons, killing some and slowing growth. Stevens Rehen's group showed Zika stunts human brain organoids.

scenes.visual: Schematic: within the same layered cortical organoid in the dish, small viral particles labelled 'Zika (2016)' concentrate heavily on the inner progenitor ring while mostly sparing outer young neurons; several progenitors fade away, remaining divisions slow, and the whole three-dimensional organoid shrinks compared to an outline of an uninfected control (Ming, Song, Tang; Rehen).

scenes.tts: Third, organoids exposed cells too scarce to study alone. Enterochromaffin cells are under one percent of the gut lining. Yet they make more than ninety percent of the body's serotonin. In 2017, Bellono and colleagues genetically tagged them in mouse intestinal organoids and checked native tissue. Across organs, mini-organs reveal tissue rules without replacing a whole body.

scenes.visual: Schematic: the dish transforms back into a coiled mouse mini-intestine; out of a ring of lining cells, a single rare enterochromaffin cell lights up bright gold with a genetic tag beside two schematic bars ('<1% of cells' and '>90% of serotonin', Bellono et al., 2017), then matches a glowing cell inside a native gut strip as the faint whole-body outline remains separate.
